metadata.title: Reading achievements among students in the United Arab Emirates: A multilevel analysis of PIRLS 2021
metadata.venue: International Journal of Educational Research Open

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2021 microdata for fourth-grade reading achievement in the United Arab Emirates, extracted via the publicly available PIRLS database and merged using IDB Analyzer (which generates SPSS syntax accounting for the complex sampling design). However, the manuscript does not report the specific PIRLS student weight variable name(s) (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) nor whether the authors applied them in estimation. The analysis is conducted with hierarchical linear modeling (lme4 in R) rather than ML algorithms, and the paper does not describe any replicate-weight variance estimation (e.g., BRR/jackknife). Therefore, readers should treat the reported standard errors and significance tests as dependent on the authors’ default handling of the complex design as implemented in the IDB Analyzer/SPSS syntax, but the exact weighting approach is not transparent.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is described as the PIRLS 2021 reading achievement score, but the manuscript does not specify whether this score is based on plausible values (PV) and, if so, how PVs were combined (e.g., Rubin’s rules vs. PV averaging). Because the paper also does not report any missing-data strategy (e.g., complete-case deletion or multiple imputation), the missing-data handling is a reporting gap that prevents replication of the exact analytic sample and uncertainty quantification.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The authors used PIRLS 2021 data for the United Arab Emirates and restricted the analytic sample to students tested in English only (20,537 students in 507 schools). Although the UAE PIRLS dataset includes fifth-grade students nested within 663 schools, the study focuses on the English-language assessment subset. No additional inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., complete-case only, missing questionnaire items, or outlier trimming) are explicitly described in the provided text.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical linear models (maximum likelihood). Level-1 model: gender beta = -5.44 (t(3599) = -2.27, p < .05); SES beta = 23.19 (t(3599) = 10.41, p < .001); confidence beta = 42.16 (t(3599) = 26.43, p < .001); engagement beta = 13.17 (t(3599) = 4.62, p < .001). Full Level-2 model: gender beta = -5.61 (t(3594) = -2.35, p < .05); SES beta = 22.51 (t(3594) = 10.14, p < .001); confidence beta = 42.37 (t(3594) = 26.65, p < .001); engagement beta = 12.70 (t(3594) = 4.47, p < .001); teacher sends to library beta = 8.88 (t(3594) = 4.70, p < .001); school character beta = 47.88 (t(3594) = 8.83, p < .001). Explained variance: 21% at Level 1 and 61% at Level 2 in the final model; ICC decreases from 0.43 (unconditional) to 0.27 (full Level-2).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2021 Grade 4 Reading (UAE, English-language test) the study leveraged socioeconomic status, students’ confidence in reading, students’ engagement in reading, gender, and teacher library-sending practices to predict reading achievement, finding that higher SES, greater reading confidence, and higher reading engagement were positively associated with achievement, while girls outperformed boys. At the school level, teacher sending students to the library and overall school character were significant positive correlates, whereas teacher reading for enjoyment, having a library in school, and principal experience were not significant in the full model. This indicates that strengthening home literacy resources and building students’ reading confidence/engagement—alongside operationalizing library access through teacher routines—may improve reading outcomes, though the multilevel design is correlational and does not establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PIRLS 2021 Grade 4 reading achievement for the United Arab Emirates, restricting the sample to students who took the English-language test (20,537 students in 507 schools). Using a multilevel (hierarchical linear) modeling approach with an unconditional model, a Level-1 student model, and a full Level-2 model, the authors estimate maximum-likelihood coefficients for student- and school-level questionnaire variables. In the final full Level-2 model, socioeconomic status, students’ confidence in reading, and students’ engagement in reading show strong positive associations with reading achievement (e.g., confidence beta = 42.37, p < .001), and girls outperform boys (beta = -5.61, p < .05). At the school level, teacher sending students to the library (beta = 8.88, p < .001) and school character (beta = 47.88, p < .001) are significant, while other school variables are not. The paper does not report a missing-data strategy or explicit PV combination rules, limiting replicability and interpretation of uncertainty.
